strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and underexplored problem: learning delay-robust policies purely from delay-free offline data, combining the offline RL and delayed RL challenges in a novel way.

Provides a theoretically grounded derivation connecting augmented-state policy iteration to a belief-based policy iteration via Wasserstein-distance bounds, including a monotonic improvement guarantee (Prop. 4.3).

Clear articulation of why naive two-stage (train belief then freeze) pipelines fail, backed by intuitive arguments (biased value targets, distribution mismatch, sample inefficiency) and correlated with empirical results.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three MuJoCo locomotion tasks, four D4RL dataset types, and both deterministic and stochastic delays of varying magnitude (4/8/16 steps), which is a fairly extensive sweep for this setting.
Reasonable set of constructed baselines (Augmented-BC, Augmented-CQL, Belief-CQL) that isolate the contributions of augmentation vs. belief modeling vs. the proposed joint optimization.
weaknesses: The core theoretical lemmas (4.1, 4.2) are directly imported from prior work [49]; the paper's theoretical contribution is largely a re-derivation/adaptation rather than fundamentally new theory, and the authors themselves admit no formal offline sample-complexity guarantees are established (Remark 4.5), limiting the rigor behind the claimed efficiency benefits.

The method assumes a known, fixed maximum delay length Δ at both training and deployment, and also assumes prior knowledge of whether the MDP is deterministic or stochastic (to choose MSE vs. MLE belief training); this is a significant practical limitation not adequately stressed until the conclusion.

Results tables report single-run scores with no standard deviations or confidence intervals, making it impossible to assess statistical significance of the reported gaps, especially given some baselines (e.g., Belief-CQL) occasionally match or exceed DT-CORL.

The narrative sometimes overstates the results — e.g., claiming DT-CORL "consistently surpasses" baselines in the stochastic setting while the same section reports it only wins/ties in 27 of 36 (75%) configurations, and Belief-CQL outperforms DT-CORL in several medium/medium-replay stochastic cases.

Evaluation is restricted to D4RL MuJoCo locomotion; no experiments on higher-dimensional, vision-based, or real robotic tasks are provided, despite motivating the work with robotics/autonomous-system latency concerns.

No ablation isolating the belief-prediction accuracy itself (e.g., prediction error vs. delay length) or the individual contributions of n-step returns/Retrace(λ), multi-step belief rollout, and the quadratic BC-style regularizer, making it hard to attribute performance gains to specific design choices.

All three baselines are constructed by the authors themselves rather than adapted from established delayed-RL methods (e.g., VDPO, BPQL, DFBT) retrofitted to the offline setting, which weakens the strength of the empirical comparison.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and underexplored problem: bridging offline RL (trained on delay-free data) with delayed online deployment, which is highly relevant for sim-to-real robotics.

Provides a theoretical derivation connecting the constrained offline policy iteration in an augmented delayed MDP to a belief-based policy iteration in the original state space, including a monotonic-improvement proposition with proof in the appendix.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning three D4RL locomotion environments, four dataset types (expert, medium, medium-replay, medium-expert), and multiple deterministic (4/8/16) and stochastic (U(1,k)) delay settings.
Reasonable set of baselines (Augmented-BC, Augmented-CQL, Belief-CQL) that isolate the contributions of state augmentation vs. belief modeling vs. the proposed joint belief-aware policy iteration.

Clear qualitative discussion of why a naive two-stage (train belief, then freeze and run offline RL) pipeline is expected to suffer from biased value targets and distribution mismatch, motivating the end-to-end design.
weaknesses: No error bars, standard deviations, or multiple-seed results are reported anywhere in Tables 1–2, making it impossible to assess the statistical significance of the reported gains, especially given several close or mixed results (e.g., Belief-CQL beats DT-CORL in a non-trivial fraction of cells: only 27/36 stochastic configurations favor DT-CORL, and no equivalent win-rate is reported for the deterministic case).

The core theoretical results (Lemma 4.1, Lemma 4.2, the performance-difference lemma in App. A.1) are directly imported from prior work [49], with the paper's contribution being largely a re-derivation/combination rather than new theory; the paper's own Remark 4.5 explicitly concedes that a rigorous offline-specific analysis is left as future work.

Remark 4.4 notes that for deterministic MDPs (which include all the MuJoCo D4RL tasks tested), the belief becomes an injective/error-free mapping and reward/next-state terms reduce to the ground-truth delay-free values; this substantially simplifies the setting being empirically evaluated and may make the reported gains less representative of genuinely stochastic or noisy real-world delay scenarios, which are only tested via a synthetic uniform-delay-length distribution rather than actual environment stochasticity.

The method assumes the maximum delay ∆ is known and fixed during training/belief-model construction; this is a strong practical assumption not clearly justified relative to real deployment where the delay distribution may be unknown or non-stationary, and the paper's own conclusion admits this limitation without proposing or testing a mitigation.

The related-work and baseline comparisons are narrowly centered on the authors' own prior papers (repeated citations to [47, 48, 49], likely self-citations), with no comparison to other belief-based delayed-RL methods such as DATS, D-Dreamer, or D-SAC, nor to any offline-to-online delay-adaptation baseline, limiting confidence that DT-CORL's advantage generalizes beyond the specific baselines constructed by the authors.

Claims of 'slashing learning inefficiency' relative to augmentation approaches are not backed by any quantitative sample-efficiency or wall-clock training-time comparison; only qualitative dimensional arguments (O(∆) blow-up) are given.

Evaluation is restricted to low-dimensional MuJoCo locomotion; no validation on higher-dimensional or vision-based tasks is provided, despite the paper's motivating framing around real-world robotic/embodied deployment and sim-to-real transfer.

The paper does not report any real hardware or physically realistic delay experiments, so the central motivating claim of 'bridging the sim-to-real latency gap' remains only indirectly supported by simulated D4RL experiments with synthetic delay injection.

strengths: Addresses a novel and practically relevant problem: learning delay-robust policies purely from delay-free offline data, bridging offline RL and delayed RL literatures that have mostly been studied separately (existing delayed RL work assumes online interaction).

Provides a theoretical derivation connecting the augmented-state constrained policy iteration formulation to a belief-based policy iteration in the original state space, including a proposition establishing monotonic Q-value improvement under the proposed scheme.

Extensive empirical evaluation spanning AntMaze goal-conditioned tasks, MuJoCo locomotion, and Adroit dexterous manipulation, under both deterministic and stochastic delay regimes and multiple delay magnitudes (4/8/16, and further 32/64 in appendix).

Useful ablation studies: comparison of belief architectures (transformer vs. ensemble MLP vs. diffusion) with accuracy/speed trade-offs, effect of offline data availability, and joint vs. separately pretrained belief training, which support the core design choices.

Reasonably thorough reproducibility materials: detailed hyperparameter tables, compute/time information, and an explicit reproducibility statement (though the code repository link appears to be missing/broken in the text).
weaknesses: On the harder AntMaze tasks (medium-play, large-play), all methods including DT-CORL perform near zero, substantially undermining the practical significance of the claimed gains in the goal-conditioned setting; the paper acknowledges this but does not investigate the cause or propose remedies.

The theoretical contribution largely reuses existing lemmas (Wu et al., 2024b) for performance-difference and Q-value bounds; the derivation from augmented PI to belief-based PI (Appendix B.1) is a fairly mechanical substitution, and the treatment of multiple Wasserstein regularization terms as being 'combined with appropriate choice of α/α2' is hand-wavy and not rigorously justified, weakening confidence in the formal soundness of Eq. (3)-(4).

Remark 4.5 explicitly states that a formal sample-complexity analysis for the offline setting is left as an open problem, so the practical implications of the theory for the paper's actual claims (sample efficiency benefits of belief vs. augmentation) remain unproven.

The DBPT-SAC baseline achieves literally 0.0 across essentially all AntMaze settings, which appears extreme and raises questions about whether it was configured/tuned fairly for this comparison; such a degenerate baseline weakens the persuasiveness of the comparison.

The method assumes a known, fixed (or effectively fixed) delay at deployment; handling of variable/stochastic delay is reduced to treating it as an 'effective fixed delay,' which is a significant simplification not carefully justified, and the paper explicitly defers unknown/time-varying/heterogeneous delays to future work.

Some experimental writing/formatting issues remain (e.g., a garbled sentence 'we vary the proportion... 25As shown in Table 4' suggesting missing text/values), and the reproducibility statement references a code repository without an actual link, limiting verifiability.

Baseline comparisons for the offline setting are all self-constructed (Augmented-BC/CQL/COMBO, Belief-CQL/IQL) rather than adaptations of established strong offline delayed-RL baselines from prior literature, making it harder to assess how the proposed method compares to alternative reasonable designs one might construct.

Limited discussion of failure cases beyond AntMaze medium/large-play, and no analysis of when/why belief estimation might fail catastrophically (e.g., under highly stochastic dynamics or large delay-to-episode-length ratios) beyond the reported average metrics.
